text: Ice at the South Pole is nearly three kilometres thick
as_written: the ice is nearly three kilometres thick
source: US Antarctic Program / National Science Foundation, South Pole Station facts (surface elevation about 2,835 m, ice roughly 2,700-2,850 m thick)

text: Antarctic ice has existed for millions of years
as_written: has not seen open sky for millions of years
source: Zachos et al. 2001, Science, 'Trends, Rhythms, and Aberrations in Global Climate'; Antarctic glaciation began about 34 million years ago

text: The Antarctic ice sheet holds more than 26 million cubic kilometres of ice
as_written: more than twenty-six million cubic kilometres of ice
source: Fretwell et al. 2013, The Cryosphere (Bedmap2); Morlighem et al. 2020, Nature Geoscience (BedMachine Antarctica)

text: Antarctica holds about 90 percent of Earth's ice
as_written: about ninety percent of all the ice on Earth
source: US National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), All About Glaciers / Antarctic ice sheet

text: Antarctic ice is around 70 percent of Earth's fresh water
as_written: around seventy percent of all its fresh water
source: US Geological Survey, Water Science School; NSIDC

text: Latent heat of fusion of ice is about 334 kJ per kg
as_written: about three hundred and thirty-four kilojoules for every kilogram
source: Standard physical constant, NIST / CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics

text: Melting the sheet requires roughly 8 times 10 to the 24 joules, derived from volume, ice density 917 kg per cubic metre, and latent heat
as_written: roughly eight trillion trillion joules
source: Derived calculation from Morlighem et al. 2020 / Fretwell et al. 2013 ice volume, ice density, and NIST latent heat

text: Global primary energy use is roughly 600 exajoules per year
as_written: roughly six hundred exajoules of energy in a year
source: Energy Institute, Statistical Review of World Energy

text: Melting the sheet would take more than ten thousand years of global energy use, derived by dividing the energy needed by annual consumption
as_written: more than ten thousand years of that
source: Derived from Energy Institute Statistical Review and the latent heat calculation above

text: Ten thousand years of human energy use is the figure borrowed in the thought experiment
as_written: borrowing ten thousand years of human energy use
source: Derived, same calculation as above

text: Antarctica covers about 14 million square kilometres, larger than Europe
as_written: about fourteen million square kilometres, which is larger than Europe
source: British Antarctic Survey; NSIDC

text: Average ice thickness is more than 2 kilometres
as_written: more than two kilometres thick
source: NSIDC; Fretwell et al. 2013 (Bedmap2)

text: Full melt would raise global sea level by nearly 58 metres
as_written: nearly fifty-eight metres
source: Morlighem et al. 2020, Nature Geoscience (BedMachine Antarctica), 57.9 m sea-level equivalent

text: West Antarctica holds a little over 4 metres of sea level equivalent
as_written: a little over four metres of sea level
source: Fretwell et al. 2013, The Cryosphere (Bedmap2), about 4.3 m

text: A canyon under Denman Glacier reaches about 3.5 km below sea level, the deepest known point on land
as_written: about three and a half kilometres below sea level
source: Morlighem et al. 2020, Nature Geoscience (BedMachine Antarctica)

text: Ice shrinks about 8 percent on melting, since ice density is about 917 kg per cubic metre against 1000 for water
as_written: a loss of about eight percent
source: Standard physical constants for ice and water density, NIST

text: About 24 million cubic kilometres of liquid water results
as_written: about twenty-four million cubic kilometres of liquid
source: Derived from ice volume and density ratio, Fretwell et al. 2013 / Morlighem et al. 2020

text: Spread evenly over the continent, the water would be more than 1.5 km deep
as_written: more than one and a half kilometres deep
source: Derived: roughly 24 million cubic km divided by about 14 million square km

text: Coldest ground-level thermometer air temperature recorded is minus 89.2 C at Vostok, 1983
as_written: minus eighty-nine point two degrees Celsius, recorded at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983
source: World Meteorological Organization, Weather and Climate Extremes Archive

text: The ice sheet's mass is more than 20 million billion tonnes
as_written: more than twenty million billion tonnes of it
source: Derived from ice volume times density, Fretwell et al. 2013 / Morlighem et al. 2020

text: Sea surface near a large ice sheet is raised by some tens of metres by gravitational attraction
as_written: by some tens of metres
source: Clark and Lingle 1977; Mitrovica et al. 2001, Nature, 'Recent mass balance of polar ice sheets inferred from patterns of global sea-level change'

text: Changes in gravity propagate at the speed of light
as_written: changes in gravity travel at the speed of light
source: General relativity; confirmed by LIGO/Virgo GW170817 observations

text: The Amazon discharges roughly 200,000 cubic metres per second
as_written: roughly two hundred thousand cubic metres every second
source: NASA Earth Observatory / Brazilian National Water Agency (ANA) discharge records, about 209,000 m3/s

text: At that rate, 24 million cubic km would take nearly 4,000 years
as_written: would take nearly four thousand years
source: Derived from Amazon discharge and meltwater volume

text: Deep-ocean tsunamis travel up to about 800 km per hour
as_written: up to roughly eight hundred kilometres an hour
source: NOAA National Tsunami Warning Center / NOAA Tsunami FAQ

text: The South Pole is about 10,000 km from the equator
as_written: about ten thousand kilometres from the equator
source: Original metre definition (one ten-millionth of the pole to equator quadrant); geodesy

text: At 800 km/h, 10,000 km takes about 12 hours
as_written: takes about twelve hours
source: Derived arithmetic

text: West Antarctic collapse would give North American coasts about 25 percent more rise than the global average
as_written: roughly a quarter more rise than the global average
source: Mitrovica, Gomez and Clark 2009, Science, 'The Sea-Level Fingerprint of West Antarctic Collapse'

text: Fifty-eight metres is about the height of a twenty-storey building
as_written: the height of a twenty-storey building
source: Approximate building-height arithmetic at about 3 m per storey

text: More than 600 million people live on land less than 10 metres above sea level
as_written: More than six hundred million people already live on land less than ten metres above sea level
source: McGranahan, Balk and Anderson 2007, Environment and Urbanization; Neumann et al. 2015, PLOS ONE

text: The highest natural point in the Maldives is about 2.4 metres
as_written: only about two and a half metres above the sea
source: CIA World Factbook, Maldives elevation extremes (2.4 m)

text: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level
as_written: About a quarter of the Netherlands already lies below sea level
source: Government of the Netherlands / Statistics Netherlands (CBS), about 26 percent

text: Florida's highest natural point is about 105 metres
as_written: about one hundred and five metres
source: US Geological Survey, Britton Hill (345 ft)

text: Florida's average elevation is about 30 metres
as_written: only about thirty metres
source: US Geological Survey, elevations and distances in the United States

text: The oceans hold about 1.3 billion cubic kilometres of water
as_written: about one point three billion cubic kilometres of water
source: NOAA National Geophysical Data Center; USGS Water Science School

text: 24 million cubic km added to the oceans is an increase of about 1.8 percent
as_written: an increase of about one point eight percent
source: Derived from NOAA ocean volume and meltwater volume

text: A 2023 Nature study projected Antarctic bottom water overturning slowing about 40 percent by 2050 under high emissions
as_written: could slow by around forty percent by 2050
source: Li, England et al. 2023, Nature, 'Abyssal ocean overturning slowdown and warming driven by Antarctic meltwater'

text: Fresh snow reflects 80 to 90 percent of sunlight
as_written: reflects eighty to ninety percent of the sunlight
source: NSIDC, Albedo and sea ice

text: Antarctica lost about 2,720 billion tonnes of ice between 1992 and 2017
as_written: about two thousand seven hundred and twenty billion tonnes of ice between 1992 and 2017
source: IMBIE team 2018, Nature, 'Mass balance of the Antarctic Ice Sheet from 1992 to 2017'

text: That loss raised sea level by 7.6 millimetres
as_written: seven point six millimetres
source: IMBIE team 2018, Nature

text: Loss rate in 2012-2017 was about 219 billion tonnes per year
as_written: about two hundred and nineteen billion tonnes a year
source: IMBIE team 2018, Nature

text: At that rate, melting the full sheet would take over 100,000 years
as_written: more than a hundred thousand years
source: Derived: ice mass of roughly 24 million gigatonnes divided by 219 gigatonnes per year

text: Thwaites Glacier is about the size of Florida
as_written: about the size of Florida
source: International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration (ITGC)

text: Thwaites holds enough ice for about 65 centimetres of sea level rise
as_written: roughly sixty-five centimetres
source: International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration (ITGC) / British Antarctic Survey

text: Thwaites collapse could destabilise neighbours for a total approaching 3 metres
as_written: a total approaching three metres
source: International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration (ITGC)

text: DeConto and Pollard 2016 projected over a metre of Antarctic sea level contribution by 2100 under highest emissions
as_written: more than a metre of sea level by 2100
source: DeConto and Pollard 2016, Nature, 'Contribution of Antarctica to past and future sea-level rise'

text: The same paper projected about 15 metres by 2500
as_written: about fifteen metres by 2500
source: DeConto and Pollard 2016, Nature

text: A 2019 paper found the cliff collapse mechanism was not needed to match the past and gave lower projections
as_written: A later paper in 2019
source: Edwards et al. 2019, Nature, 'Revisiting Antarctic ice loss due to marine ice-cliff instability'

text: Meltwater pulse 1A about 14,600 years ago raised sea level roughly 14 to 18 metres in under 500 years; the source is debated
as_written: About fourteen thousand six hundred years ago, sea level rose roughly fourteen to eighteen metres in under five hundred years
source: Deschamps et al. 2012, Nature, 'Ice-sheet collapse and sea-level rise at the Bolling warming 14,600 years ago'

text: Burning all fossil fuel reserves could nearly eliminate the Antarctic ice sheet over thousands of years
as_written: could be nearly eliminated, over thousands of years
source: Winkelmann et al. 2015, Science Advances, 'Combustion of available fossil fuel resources sufficient to eliminate the Antarctic Ice Sheet'

text: Antarctica glaciated about 34 million years ago at the Eocene-Oligocene transition
as_written: Around thirty-four million years ago
source: Zachos et al. 2001, Science; DeConto and Pollard 2003, Nature

text: Palm pollen found in Antarctic seabed cores dates to around 50 million years ago
as_written: dated to around fifty million years ago
source: Pross et al. 2012, Nature, 'Persistent near-tropical warmth on the Antarctic continent during the early Eocene epoch'

text: About 3 million years ago, in the Pliocene, CO2 was similar to today's and sea level was many metres higher, with estimates ranging from a few to over twenty metres
as_written: around three million years ago in the Pliocene
source: Dutton et al. 2015, Science, 'Sea-level rise due to polar ice-sheet mass loss during past warm periods'; Miller et al. 2012, Geology

text: Bedrock in the Amundsen Sea region is rising at up to 41 mm per year
as_written: up to forty-one millimetres a year
source: Barletta et al. 2018, Science, 'Observed rapid bedrock uplift in Amundsen Sea Embayment promotes ice-sheet stability'

text: Models suggest post-melt rebound of hundreds of metres, depending heavily on mantle viscosity
as_written: could rise by hundreds of metres over thousands of years
source: Whitehouse et al. 2019, Nature Communications, 'Solid Earth change and the evolution of the Antarctic Ice Sheet'

text: Redistributing polar ice mass toward the oceans slows Earth's rotation and lengthens the day; full melt would lengthen it by a fraction of a second
as_written: lengthen the day by a fraction of a second
source: Derived moment-of-inertia estimate; see Agnew 2024, Nature

text: Polar ice melt delayed the possible need for a negative leap second by about three years, to 2029
as_written: by about three years, to 2029
source: Agnew 2024, Nature, 'A global timekeeping problem postponed by global warming'

text: More than 400 subglacial lakes lie beneath the Antarctic ice
as_written: more than four hundred lakes
source: Siegert et al. 2016, Journal of Glaciology, 'Advances in the inventory and understanding of Antarctic subglacial lakes'

text: The Gamburtsev Mountains are comparable in size and shape to the European Alps and were revealed by radar in the late 2000s
as_written: about the size and shape of the European Alps
source: Bo et al. 2009, Nature, 'The Gamburtsev mountains revealed by airborne radar'; AGAP / International Polar Year survey 2008-2009
